titel: Goal Setting Worksheet: One Goal, One Weekly Plan
h1: A Goal Setting Worksheet You Can Actually Use This Week
desc: Copy this free goal setting worksheet to choose one priority, plan a specific action, handle an obstacle, and review what happened each week.
antwoord: A useful goal setting worksheet connects something you want with an action you can take, a situation that will remind you, and a way to check what happened. Copy the prompts below into a notebook or document. Start with one goal and plan one week of actions. This is a practical planning aid, not a promise that a worksheet will produce results or change your life in seven days.

secties.kop: 1. Decide what this worksheet needs to help you do
alineas: Start with a decision you have already been avoiding: which goal deserves attention now? Writing ten wishes on a page can feel productive while leaving tomorrow unchanged. For this worksheet, choose one priority for the next review period. Other goals can stay on a separate list. You are giving this goal a working slot, not declaring that everything else is unimportant.

Write the outcome in ordinary language. For example, you might want to finish a first draft, practice a new skill, or make steady progress on a personal project. Then ask what would count as visible progress. A clear description is more useful here than an impressive sentence you cannot check.

If you are still deciding what to keep or change in your life, use the separate seven-day reset guide first. If you have a backlog of appointments and unfinished admin, the life admin checklist answers a different question. This page starts after you have chosen something you want to work toward.

secties.kop: 2. Separate the outcome from the action
alineas: An outcome is what you hope will happen. An action is what you will do. Finishing a short story is an outcome. Drafting one scene after breakfast is an action. You can choose the action even when you cannot guarantee that the finished story will be good, published, or praised.

Choose an action small enough to describe without using the words 'try harder.' State what you will start, where you will do it, and how you will know the attempt happened. Keep the size realistic for an ordinary busy day. A challenging goal does not require every individual session to be difficult.

Use two separate checks: one for carrying out the action and one for progress toward the outcome. Completing several writing sessions may not immediately finish a story. That is a reason to review the approach, not to pretend the outcome has already happened.

These prompts are our own practical template. They are not a validated assessment. Copy them into a document, write them by hand, or print this page using your browser. The lines are spaces for your answers, not fields that save information on this website.
Use one sheet for one goal. A week is simply a convenient review interval in this example. Choose a different interval if your project produces useful feedback more slowly.
lijst: Why this matters to me now: ____________________
What visible progress would look like: ____________________
What I can do, even though I cannot guarantee the outcome: ____________________
When and where I will start it: ____________________
The situation that will remind me: ____________________
If that situation happens, then I will: ____________________
The obstacle I can reasonably anticipate: ____________________
If that obstacle appears, my smaller or alternative action is: ____________________
The evidence I will record after an attempt: ____________________
What I will deliberately leave off this week's plan: ____________________

alineas: Imagine that you want to finish the first draft of a short story. Your visible outcome might be a complete beginning, middle, and ending that you can revise. Your next action could be writing the opening scene. There is no need to decide on a publishing strategy before you have tried that action.

Your plan might read: after I put my breakfast dishes away on Tuesday and Thursday, I will sit at the kitchen table and write for ten minutes. Before those days, I will leave the draft document open and write one sentence describing the scene I want to begin. These are illustrative choices, not a research-backed optimum for writing.

An obstacle plan could be: if the kitchen is too noisy, I will use my headphones and draft three sentences in a notebook in another room. If the available time disappears completely, I will decide on a new opportunity rather than quietly doubling the next session.

Your record can stay simple: Tuesday, started, wrote 140 rough words; Thursday, did not start, unexpected work call. The word count is information about this example. It is not a universal target. At review time, look at both the actions attempted and what the story actually needs next.

secties.kop: 5. Review the evidence without grading your character
alineas: At the review date, read what you recorded before making a new plan. Ask whether the cue occurred, whether you noticed it, whether the action was possible, and whether it moved the project forward. 'I am bad at goals' does not tell you which of those steps needs changing.

If you repeatedly forgot to start, consider a more noticeable cue. If the action was too large for the available slot, reduce its size or choose a different slot. If you completed it but made little useful progress, reconsider the action itself. These are options to test, not diagnoses of why a particular person struggled.

Change one part of the plan when you can. Keeping the other parts steady makes it easier to understand what happened next. Keep a note of your previous plan instead of rewriting history as though the new version had always been your intention.
lijst: What changed in the project, separately from how busy I felt? ____________________
What obstacle appeared more than once? ____________________
What will I keep next time? ____________________
What one part will I adjust? ____________________

secties.kop: 6. What research supports, and what this worksheet adds
alineas: Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 research review examines implementation intentions: plans that connect a situation with a response. It supports considering a concrete when, where, or if-then plan alongside an intention. It does not establish that our particular worksheet, session length, or weekly schedule will work for every reader.

Harkin and colleagues' 2016 meta-analysis examined experiments that encouraged people to monitor goal progress. On average, monitoring interventions improved goal attainment. The findings support making progress visible enough to review, while leaving room for different goals, settings, and results.

The prompts, short-story example, and one-sheet layout on this page are our own application of those ideas. The papers did not test this page or the Lasting Change Workbook. A record can reveal a problem; it cannot remove every constraint on your time, resources, or opportunities.

secties.kop: 7. Use a workbook only if you want a longer record
alineas: You can use the worksheet above without buying anything. A notebook or document is enough to record a plan and review it. If your chosen goal involves practicing one repeatable behavior and you want a longer paper record, the Lasting Change Workbook is an optional next step.

Use the paperback option shown on this page if it suits you. This guide does not offer a downloadable paid workbook checkout or promise an email sequence. The useful first step is completing your own sheet, then testing the action you wrote down.

faq: What should a goal setting worksheet include?

Include one goal, a description of visible progress, a specific action, a cue or planned opportunity, an obstacle response, and a review date. Keep the action you control separate from the outcome you hope to achieve.
Is this a SMART goals worksheet?

It is a practical planning sheet rather than a complete SMART framework. You can use a specific, checkable goal with it. Its distinctive parts are linking the goal to an action, anticipating an obstacle, and reviewing actual evidence.
Can I use the worksheet for more than one goal?

Yes, but use a separate sheet for each goal and check that the actions fit your real schedule. Do not give every goal the same time slot. If the plans compete, choose which one takes priority this week.
Can I download a fillable PDF here?

This version provides copyable prompts on the page. It is not a fillable PDF or an online form that saves your answers. Copy the template into your own document or notebook, or use your browser's print function.
What if I did not do the planned action?

Record what happened without converting it into a character judgment. Check the cue, timing, size of the action, and practical obstacles. Adjust one part of the next plan where possible. A missed attempt is information, not evidence that no future plan can work.
